summary: Dimethicone (dimeticone; its activated form combined with silica is simeticone) is an inert, silicone-based antifoaming agent used orally as an antiflatulent for trapped wind, bloating, the gas symptoms of dyspepsia and IBS, and infant colic, and to disperse gas before abdominal imaging or endoscopy. It works purely by a physical action - lowering the surface tension of gas bubbles so they coalesce and are passed - and is not absorbed from the gut, has essentially no systemic effects, drug interactions, or organ-dose adjustments, and is regarded as very safe (including in pregnancy and lactation). It is also used topically as a skin barrier/emollient and, as a 4% lotion, to treat head lice by physically coating and suffocating them. It is an OTC/established agent, not an FDA new-drug-approved prescription product.
indications: Relief of flatulence, trapped wind, abdominal bloating and the gas-related symptoms of dyspepsia (and gas symptoms in IBS)
Dispersal of gas/foam before abdominal radiography, endoscopy or colonoscopy

moa: Dimeticone/simeticone is an antifoaming agent that lowers the surface tension of gas and mucus-trapped bubbles in the gastrointestinal tract, causing small bubbles to coalesce into larger ones that are more easily passed (by belching or as flatus) or absorbed. The effect is purely physical, not pharmacological. As a head-lice agent the lotion acts physically, coating the louse and disrupting its water/respiratory balance to immobilise and kill it (effective even against insecticide-resistant lice).

absolute: Hypersensitivity to simeticone/dimeticone or any excipient
relative: Combination products carry the contraindications of their other ingredients (e.g. antacid salts), not of dimeticone itself
monitor: Seek medical advice if GI symptoms persist beyond about 2 weeks

preg: Considered safe. Dimeticone/simeticone is not absorbed - it works only in the gut and does not enter the bloodstream - so no harm is expected in pregnancy. Check any co-ingredients in combination products.
lact: Considered safe. It is not absorbed and does not get into breast milk, so it can be used while breastfeeding.
renal: No dose adjustment is required - the agent is not absorbed and is excreted unchanged.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required - the agent is not absorbed and is excreted unchanged.

minor: Levothyroxine - simeticone may theoretically reduce its absorption; separate dosing as a precaution
interactions.food: Best taken after meals and at bedtime; no clinically significant food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: No systemic interaction; alcohol-containing head-lice lotions are flammable.
interactions.diagnostics: No systemic laboratory effects; used to clear foam and improve endoscopic/radiographic views.

rare: Scalp/skin or eye irritation and rare hair loss with the head-lice lotion
emergency: Signs of a serious allergic reaction (swelling of lips/mouth/throat/tongue, difficulty breathing, widespread rash)

monitoring: Reassess if oral GI symptoms persist beyond about 2 weeks or infant colic worsens
Report suspected reactions via pharmacovigilance schemes

pearls: Purely physical antifoaming action - inert, not absorbed, so essentially no systemic effects, interactions, or organ dose adjustments
Symptomatic relief only; it does not reduce gas production
Take after meals and at bedtime; separate from levothyroxine
The 4% dimeticone lotion treats head lice by physically coating/suffocating them and works even against insecticide-resistant lice (repeat after 7 days)
Not FDA new-drug-approved as a prescription drug - an OTC/established antiflatulent and head-lice/skin-barrier agent
missed: If a dose is missed, take it when remembered with the next meal; do not double up. It is used symptomatically, so doses can simply be taken as needed.
overdose: No toxicity is expected - the substance is inert and not absorbed, with no recognised overdose syndrome. Accidental ingestion of the head-lice lotion has no specific safety concern; provide supportive/symptomatic care only.
